newsitem.title: USA: IMF official confident of eventual gold sales pact.
newsitem.headline: IMF official confident of eventual gold sales pact.

text.p: A senior International Monetary Fund official voiced confidence on Monday that the IMF will approve "down the road" a controversial proposal to sell some of its gold to aid the world's poor.

"There is in the executive board a needed majority to consider ... sales of gold," the senior official, who declined to be named, told reporters ahead of the start of the IMF/World Bank annual meeting here later this week.
The IMF board last week put off a decision on the proposal, instead opting to ask member nations for bilateral contributions first to finance stepped-up aid for the poor.

The IMF needs some $3.5 billion early next century to finance a continuation of its Enhanced Structural Adjustment (lending) Facility (ESAF) and its participation in a multilateral debt relief initiative for poor countries.

The senior IMF official said he was "highly satisfied" with the response of member nations to the Fund's request for bilateral contributions. But he added those contributions will probably not be enough to completely close the financing gap.

IMF management, backed by the United States, Britain and most other member nations, had proposed selling up to five million of the Fund's nearly 104 million ounces of gold if needed to help finance stepped-up aid for poor countries.
But a few nations -- Germany, Italy and Switzerland -- opposed the proposal, arguing in part that the IMF should not sell gold except in cases of extreme financial emergency.
The IMF official, though, said he was confident that the Fund would be able to reach a broad consensus on the proposal at some point in the future.
"We have made enough progress to ... to make sure ... we would, down the road, at the needed moment, have the appropriate desirable broad consensus," he said.

The senior official said he expects the IMF's policy-setting Interim Committee to give the "green light" to the continuation of ESAF and participation in the debt relief plan at its meeting on September 29.
Creditor nations that make up the so-called Paris Club are meeting this week to consider stepping up the debt relief they provide poor nations as part of the initiative.

The IMF official predicted that the Paris Club discussions would be difficult and somewhat protracted and that it would take time to reach a decision. But he voiced confidence that any agreement would be consistent with the IMF's plans.
